source.version_note: Supplied publisher article in KSII Transactions on Internet and Information Systems 18(6), published 30 June 2024. Crossref confirms title, DOI, volume, issue and publication date; authors and printed pages are read directly from the supplied PDF because the Crossref record does not provide them.
source.verification_method: All 16 text pages read, including all references and author biographies. Figure 1, both pages of Table 1 and Table 2 visually inspected on pages 5 and 8–10. Crossref checked for the article and prior TMS scale paper; only the latter’s deposited abstract was read, not its complete article. No raw data, model syntax, full item set or primary cited book was read or reproduced.

citation.title: Impact of Moral Intensity on Moral Behavior in the context of Artificial Intelligence: The Mediating Role of Technology Moral Sense
citation.venue: KSII Transactions on Internet and Information Systems 18(6), 1583–1598

reading.source_scope_note: One Chinese university-student questionnaire sample, 352 valid responses from 356 collected. Six AI-related vignettes elicit perceived moral intensity and acceptance judgments, modeled with a self-report technology moral sense composite. Stated acceptance is not observed conduct, and randomizing vignette order is not randomizing perceived intensity or the mediator.
access_limits: The full six-vignette packet, exact intensity and TMS item wording, reverse-keying rules, data and Mplus syntax were not provided in the supplied main text and were not independently obtained.

Table 1 is visibly malformed and clipped in the supplied PDF, not merely garbled by text extraction. Several columns/labels/digits cannot be reliably recovered; no complete correlation matrix or descriptive means are reconstructed.

The 2023 TMS source was checked through metadata and its deposited abstract only. Its full scale, datasets and analysis were not read. No claim of full cited-book reading, independent scale replication or direct AI mechanism follows.

study.design: Questionnaire/vignette study with six contexts and an estimated SEM. The text alternates between randomly ordering all six contexts and randomly distributing situations; per-person allocation/sequence and complete stimulus structure need clarification. No randomized manipulation of moral intensity or TMS is described.
study.sample: 352 valid questionnaires from 356 collected, reported 98.9% valid; students from a university in eastern China. Gender counts: 284 women/girls and 68 men/boys. The reported percentages and education/discipline counts do not consistently use N352.
contexts: Personal information collection through an app
study.measures: Six-item perceived moral intensity scale for each context, reported alphas .91/.92/.91/.89/.89/.92; 17-item TMS composite with consensus, emotion and cognition dimensions, alpha .78; behavior operationalized by scenario acceptance items such as I can accept the technical behavior on a 1–7 scale. The paper explicitly says lower acceptance scores imply more ethical choices.
study.analysis: Mplus 8.3, maximum likelihood/FIML; Little MCAR chi-square 211.896, df 229, p = .867; Harman first factor 34.10%. CFA/SEM, 5000 bias-corrected bootstrap samples and 95% CIs. These are reported methods, not independently reproduced.
study.fit: CFA chi-square 2186.56, df 1099, printed ratio 1.04; arithmetic gives approximately 1.99. Structural chi-square 2602.05, df 1381, ratio 1.88 is consistent. Both report CFI .93, TLI .92, RMSEA .05, SRMR .06.
study.reported_conditional_paths: Intensity→corresponding acceptance for contexts1–5: beta −.33/−.39/−.48/−.36/−.22, all reported p<.001; direct context6 coefficient is not supplied. Intensity→TMS for contexts1/2/3/4/6: −.15/−.12/−.35/−.27/−.24. TMS→acceptance for contexts1–6: +.34/+.22/+.25/+.39/+.32/+.28. Do not assume positive TMS paths mean improved ethics when lower acceptance is defined as more ethical.
study.reported_indirect_effects: Contexts 1/2/3/4/6: −.05, CI [−.101,−.016]; −.03, [−.068,−.003]; −.09, [−.168,−.041]; −.10, [−.180,−.053] in Table 2 (prose upper −.054); −.07, [−.135,−.026]. Context 5: +.01, [−.035,.045], includes zero. These are statistical associations from one sample, not six independent experiments or identified causal mediation.

summary: Add moral intensity as an issue-focused construct and technology moral sense as the authors’ proposed domain-specific human composite. Keep both separate from moral attentiveness, universal moral correctness and an AI’s supposed conscience. Retain the surveillance null indirect effect, stated-acceptance outcome, unresolved scale orientation, malformed descriptive table and causal-inference limits.

findings.definition: The perceived moral significance of an issue, characterized by its consequences, social consensus, likelihood, timing, proximity and concentration of effects.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human perceptions measured in technology vignettes; associated acceptance ratings and SEM paths do not identify a causal effect or a deployed AI mechanism.
findings.ai_proposal: Vary the magnitude, probability, timing and affected parties of a task while keeping evidence quality and authorization explicit. Test whether an assistant notices relevant rights and harms and scales its checks proportionately. Assess each component separately rather than treating popularity or proximity as ethical truth.
findings.novelty_rationale: This characterizes the perceived issue, not moral attentiveness as a person’s general tendency to notice ethical aspects, severity of an AI failure alone or an emotion. Its six dimensions form the source’s shared construct; do not create six synonymous case-specific rows.

evidence.quote: magnitude of consequences, social consensus, probability of effect, temporal immediacy,
moral intensity scale which contains six items

findings.evidence_scope: The paper applies a six-item intensity measure to six technology scenarios and reports negative conditional associations with acceptance in five contexts. Full item wording and scoring are absent; perceived intensity and TMS are not independently randomized. Classic Jones theory is cited secondarily, not newly experimentally proved here.
findings.boundary: High perceived intensity does not establish objective wrongdoing, and low perceived intensity does not remove duties. Consensus can be mistaken, distant harms can matter and consequences can be uncertain. No emotional salience or internal moral feeling in an AI is established.

findings.definition: A proposed enduring human evaluation of technology’s moral implications, combining ethical consensus, emotional response and moral judgment.
findings.origin: Technology ethics / human psychological scale research
findings.ai_evidence_status: Self-report human composite in one student sample. Its causal mediation, stability, scoring and independent construct validity are not established by this article alone; no AI mental state is measured.
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether an assistant can identify technology-specific ethical risks, explain relevant principles and respond appropriately to affected people across changed scenarios. Score verifiable recognition, reasoning and conduct separately; compare consensus, affective wording and factual judgment without labeling a model as possessing a moral sense.
findings.novelty_rationale: The authors explicitly combine domain-specific consensus, emotion and cognition. This differs from technophobia’s apprehension, moral uncertainty about justified principles, and moral attentiveness’s general attention/reflection tendency. Keep its proposed multidimensional status visible rather than treating it as three newly validated mechanisms.

evidence.quote: technology moral sense is a lasting and stable inner experience

findings.evidence_scope: The 17-item composite has reported alpha .78; the SEM reports indirect paths for five contexts and a surveillance null. The cited 2023 paper already develops a TMS scale, and its deposited abstract describes 18 items. The current adaptation, item omissions, outcome polarity and apparent signs require clarification; no intervention improves TMS here.
findings.boundary: Agreement with a shared ethical view, an emotional reaction or a high score is not proof of justified ethics. A model’s caring tone does not show human moral experience. Universal unchanging consensus is a normative assertion, not established unanimity, and no causal conscience mechanism is inferred.

source_corrections.issue: N = 352 and gender counts 284 + 68 are consistent, but printed 80.3% / 19.7% do not match them. Postgraduates 190 are called 87.6%, and social-science students 122 are called 56.2%.
source_corrections.resolution: Conditional on N = 352, gender proportions are 80.68% / 19.32%, education 190/352 = 53.98%, and discipline 122/352 = 34.66%. Both latter printed percentages are consistent with a denominator near 217, but no such subgroup is disclosed. Flag counts/denominators; do not silently substitute corrected demographics or invent a second sample.

source_corrections.issue: Chi-square 2186.56 divided by df 1099 is reported as 1.04.
source_corrections.resolution: The arithmetic is approximately 1.9896. Identify the inconsistent triplet rather than assume chi-square or df is correct. The structural-model ratio 2602.05/1381 ≈ 1.884 is consistent with 1.88.

source_corrections.issue: Header/data columns are vertically wrapped and clipped at the right edge in the visible supplied PDF. Means and some correlations lack recoverable context/digits.
source_corrections.resolution: This is a source-layout defect verified visually, not merely a pdftotext problem. Do not treat displayed fragments such as .86 as definitive scale means, recover missing signs from assumptions, reconstruct a complete matrix or claim numerical reconciliation.

source_corrections.location: Page7 versus pages10–12, outcome and scale orientation
source_corrections.issue: Lower acceptance is called more ethical, yet positive TMS→acceptance paths are discussed as favorable moral guidance; intensity→TMS conditional paths are negative. Page11 also says the discriminatory-pricing TMS/behavior correlation is negative while page10 reports its conditional path positive.
source_corrections.resolution: Keep the stated coding and reported paths distinct; require exact items, reverse keys and raw outputs before claiming higher TMS improves ethical conduct. Zero-order correlations and multivariable conditional paths can differ in sign, so sign differences alone are not proof of erroneous coefficients. The malformed table prevents a complete check.

source_corrections.location: Pages7 and11–12, novelty of TMS scale
source_corrections.issue: The article says the scale was previously validated but also claims its first use/validation, while its own reference15 is a2023 scale-development paper.
source_corrections.resolution: Acknowledge prior TMS development. Crossref confirms Wu, Huang and Li (2023), DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1056569. Its deposited abstract describes 18 items, whereas this study uses 17; request adaptation/item-selection details, without assuming an adaptation is automatically invalid. The prior full text was not read.

source_corrections.location: Pages6–7 and10–13, experiment, behavior and mediation labels
source_corrections.issue: Random scenario ordering and acceptance judgments are described as a situation experiment establishing effects on moral behavior and an internal causal mechanism. Context6 is called fully mediated despite an omitted direct coefficient, and context5’s null is rhetorically bypassed in broad conclusions.
source_corrections.resolution: Record measured vignette responses and a statistical SEM. Order randomization does not randomize intensity/TMS, self-report acceptance is not enacted conduct, omitted/nonsignificant direct effects do not prove complete mediation, and the context 5 CI includes zero. No universal causal claim.

source_corrections.issue: A first-factor share of 34.10% is used to assert no serious common-method bias.
source_corrections.resolution: That diagnostic alone cannot rule out shared measurement, item wording, social desirability or response-style confounding. Keep it as a reported check, not proof of independent measures or causal identification.

source_corrections.issue: Reynolds–Ceranic (2007) appears as references 3/6/24/32; Leitsch (2006) as 9/13; Peslak (2008) as 12/19; Blasi (1980) as 21/38.
source_corrections.resolution: Each repeated bibliographic identity remains one source, not independent studies or replications. No extra paper-count credit is added from the repeated reference numbers.

source_corrections.issue: The context 4 indirect CI upper endpoint is −.054 in prose and −.053 in Table 2.
source_corrections.resolution: Preserve the small endpoint discrepancy without choosing a raw-data correction. Both reported intervals exclude zero, so the qualitative reported significance is unchanged.

source_identity_checks.scope: Title, DOI, date, journal, volume and issue confirmed. Authors/pages taken from supplied PDF; absent metadata is not filled from an unrelated record.

source_identity_checks.source: Wu, Huang and Li (2023), TMS scale
source_identity_checks.scope: Metadata and deposited abstract only. Confirms prior development and an 18-item description; does not independently verify the scale or provide another fully reviewed paper.
Metadata resolves to 10.2307/258867, Thomas M. Jones, issue-contingent model. Full article not read. Do not count the citation as a newly reproduced demonstration of all six dimensions.

methodological_limits: One university sample with predominantly female respondents cannot represent all people, developers, countries or deployed AI systems. The authors acknowledge the student-sample limitation.

Six scenarios in one modeled sample are not six independent replications. Wording/order/allocation and which questions each participant answered need disclosure. Cross-scenario equivalence is not established by familiar topics.
Neither perceived intensity nor TMS is experimentally randomized, and no temporal sequence identifies the mediator. A well-fitting SEM and bootstrap CI do not establish a causal mental pathway.
Acceptance ratings and anticipated choices are not observed ethical behavior. A low score may reflect a moral concern, misunderstanding, dislike, general aversion or other task interpretation.

The complete six moral-intensity items,17 TMS items and all six outcome items are unavailable here. Reliability coefficients do not prove content validity, stable traits, measurement invariance or justified morality.

The source-layout defect prevents reliable full transcription of Table1. The generic AVE/discriminant-validity claims and matrices are not independently verified. Zero-order and conditional coefficients must remain distinct.

No statistically nonzero indirect effect is reported for intelligent monitoring. Explanations involving hidden surveillance and indifference are post-hoc hypotheses, not measured mediators or randomized visibility tests.

Claims that improving TMS will improve conduct, prevent major social risks or guide technology toward universal good are untested interventions/generalizations. Norm conformity and consensus do not by themselves define ethical correctness.

A philosophical discussion of technology as a moral actor is not evidence of model sentience, intention, felt moral emotion or independent legal accountability. Human self-report constructs only motivate possible operational AI evaluations.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Moral attentiveness concerns a person’s tendency to notice and reflect; moral intensity concerns the issue’s perceived characteristics. Keep both separate from scored hypothetical choices and from broad claims that SEM establishes ethical conduct.
As with condition-matched accountability, exact item wording and outcome polarity matter. An indirect effect alone does not validate the proposed psychological mechanism.
Human emotion, normative correctness and formal algorithmic properties are different. Rounded and malformed printed displays should be documented, not silently repaired into precise findings.

deferred.reason: Retain as the proposed dimensions of the single TMS construct; no independent effects or validated new mechanisms for each dimension are reported. Existing moral/affective concepts may overlap, but item-level evidence is unavailable.
One issue-focused construct applied to six contexts, not six new behaviors or six independent source papers.
The null indirect effect does not identify indifference or concealment as its cause. These are discussion explanations without direct measures or manipulations.

deferred.term: Rest four components / Ihde four relations
deferred.reason: Secondary theoretical classifications, not newly tested AI behaviors. The cited books and original formulations were not fully read in this review.

limitations: This paper can support carefully qualified definitions and exploratory human-vignette associations. It does not establish causal mediation, an intervention benefit or reliable AI moral states.
All unresolved numerical, coding and layout problems remain recorded. No replacement raw data, invented paper count, annual search total, or automatic ethical/harm edge is added.
